Problem 94. Applying a rule with an exception: Ivy
Knowledge context.
Rules often have conditions and exceptions. Logical reading prevents us from applying a general rule when an overriding exception is active.
Given facts.

Ivy is 13 years old. A library rule says: a child may enter the archive room if age ≥ 11 AND an adult permit is present. Exception: during an evacuation drill, nobody may enter. Permit present: no. Evacuation drill: no.
Rules.
Check exceptions first if they override the general rule. Otherwise every condition joined by AND must be true.
Task.
May Ivy enter the archive room under these facts? Show which conditions succeed or fail.
Step-by-step solution.
1. Age test: 13≥11 is True. 2. Permit test is False. 3. Because the general rule uses AND, both tests must pass. 4. Therefore entry is not allowed.
Answer.
No, Ivy may not enter.
Knowledge takeaway.
The order of reasoning matters when exceptions override ordinary rules.
Formal model.
Boolean rule with priority: exception predicate first, then conjunction of eligibility conditions.

C2. Rights as limits on decisions
Problem 96. Majority rule and a protected right: case 1
Knowledge context.
Democratic procedures use voting, but constitutional systems can place some rights beyond ordinary majority power.
Given facts.

A council of 18 members votes 13 to 5 for a proposal that would forbid one named group from the right to speak at a peaceful meeting. The classroom constitution states: (1) ordinary proposals pass by simple majority; (2) an ordinary majority may not remove the listed equal rights from a group.
Rules.
A decision must satisfy both the voting procedure and the higher rights constraint. Passing a vote is not sufficient if the content violates a protected right.
Task.
Did the proposal receive a majority? May it take effect under the stated constitution?
Step-by-step solution.

1. Vote check: 13>5, so the proposal has a simple majority. 2. Content check: the proposal removes a protected equal right (speak at a peaceful meeting) from a group. 3. The higher rights rule therefore blocks the proposal even though the vote passed.
Answer.
It received a majority, but it may not take effect under the stated rights rule.
Knowledge takeaway.
A majority answers who won a vote; it does not by itself answer whether every possible decision is lawful or fair under higher rules.
Formal model.
Two-stage validity test: procedural predicate AND rights-compliance predicate.

C3. Voting, majority, and quorum
Problem 101. Quorum and majority in a 17-member committee
Knowledge context.
Voting rules often contain more than one threshold. Quorum concerns participation; majority concerns the votes cast according to the stated rule.
Given facts.

A committee has 17 members. 17 are present. Votes: yes=8, no=8, abstain=1. Rule: quorum is at least 60% of all members; if quorum exists, a motion passes when yes votes are strictly more than no votes.
Rules.
First test quorum using all members as the denominator. Only then compare yes and no; abstentions count for presence but not as no votes under this rule.
Task.
Is quorum met, and does the motion pass?
Step-by-step solution.
1. Quorum threshold=ceil(0.60×17)=11. 2. Present=17, so quorum is met. 3. Yes=8, no=8; yes>no is False. 4. Combine the two tests.
Answer.
Quorum is met; the motion does not pass.
Knowledge takeaway.
Procedural reasoning requires applying tests in the right order and using the correct denominator.
Formal model.
Threshold predicates: quorum(present,total) and majority(yes,no); pass = quorum ∧ majority.
